planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; the crisp white leaf margins hold their color best out of hot afternoon sun.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Variegated Japanese fairy bells forms tidy, upright-then-arching stems clothed in crisp, oval, parallel-veined leaves broadly edged in clean white, brightening shaded ground far more than the plain green species. Small, nodding, pale greenish-white bell flowers dangle in pairs beneath the foliage in mid-spring, followed by inconspicuous black berries in late summer. The rhizomes spread steadily but not aggressively, gradually knitting together into a handsome, slow groundcover useful for edging shaded paths or lighting up the base of hostas and ferns. Keep soil consistently moist through the growing season and topdress with compost or leaf mold annually; the variegation is more pronounced in brighter shade but the foliage can scorch in direct afternoon sun.

common_name: Green Giant Fairy Bells (Bamboo-Like Chinese Disporum)

planting.note: Plant divisions of the clumping rhizome in spring into rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in light to partial shade; give it room, since this is by far the largest fairy bells in general cultivation.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into rich, humus-laden, evenly moist soil in light to partial shade, giving plants generous room to develop their imposing, bamboo-like stature. Green Giant sends up thick, cane-like shoots in shades of pink, cream, and green each spring that mature to deep green and can reach 5 to 10 feet in a single season under good conditions, clothed in glossy, lance-shaped leaves that arch gracefully at the tips. Fragrant, branched sprays of nodding, creamy-white bell flowers open with the new spring growth, followed by glossy black berries in fall. Foliage remains evergreen in milder winters and dies back to resprout vigorously from the rootstock after hard freezes further north. Site it as a bold architectural accent or informal screen at the back of a shaded border, where its towering canes create scale rarely seen in other woodland shade perennials.

common_name: Dwarf Himalayan Solomon's Seal (Creeping Pink-Flowered Polygonatum)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike taller Solomon's seals, this dwarf alpine species resents heavy shade and dislikes soggy winter soil.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to open sun, taking care not to bury the shallow rhizomes too deeply. Dwarf Himalayan Solomon's seal is a diminutive, mat-forming alpine species from the high grasslands of the Himalaya and western China, spreading by wiry underground rhizomes into a low, dense carpet only a few inches tall. In late spring, surprisingly large, flared, lilac-pink flowers appear close to the ground, often before or alongside the narrow, glossy leaves, giving the colony a soft haze of pink quite unlike any taller Polygonatum. It is best suited to a rock garden, trough, or the front edge of a shaded raised bed rather than deep woodland shade, since good drainage and some direct light produce the densest flowering. Once established the rhizomes expand steadily to form an expanding patch that tolerates being lifted and divided every few years to control spread or share.

common_name: Striatum Solomon's Seal (Cream-Centered Variegated Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; variegation is boldest with a little morning light but stays true even in fairly deep shade, and clumps build slowly at first.

directions: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Striatum is among the most dramatically variegated of the garden Solomon's seals, with bold cream streaks running not just along the leaf margins but well into the leaf centers, giving each slightly wavy leaf a lively, hand-painted look rather than a simple edged pattern. Arching stems carry paired rows of these striped leaves above which small, dangling, white bells tipped in green appear in late spring, followed by dark berries. The variegation slows the plant's vigor compared to plain-leaved Solomon's seals, so clumps take a few seasons to bulk up into a significant colony, but the wait rewards the patient gardener with one of the showiest variegated woodland perennials available. Site it where its striking foliage can be appreciated up close, such as along a shaded path edge or beside dark-leaved companions like hellebores or hardy ferns.

common_name: Albomarginata Toad Lily (Cream-Edged Variegated Toad Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; toad lilies need consistent moisture and wilt noticeably if the soil is allowed to dry out.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Albomarginata combines the familiar late-season, orchid-like, purple-spotted flowers of hairy toad lily with the bonus of neatly cream-margined foliage, giving the plant garden interest for months before the flowers even open in leaf axils along the upper stems from late summer into fall. The narrow, creamy-white leaf edges brighten shaded plantings through the whole growing season and pair especially well with solid dark-green ferns or hostas, where the variegated foliage provides contrast long before bloom time. Arching stems reach a modest 15 to 18 inches, making this a good front-of-border toad lily. Keep the crown consistently moist through summer and mulch with leaf litter for winter protection; established clumps can be divided every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor and share.

common_name: Tojen Toad Lily (Large-Leaved Unspotted Lavender Toad Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, organically rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give this large-leaved hybrid more room than typical toad lilies to display its bold foliage.

directions: Plant in moist, organically rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Tojen stands apart from other toad lilies for its unusually large, oval to oblong, clasping leaves reaching up to 15 inches long, giving the clump a bold, almost tropical texture unlike the narrower foliage of most Tricyrtis. From late summer into fall, clusters of soft lavender, orchid-like flowers with yellow throats open at the stem tips, entirely free of the purple spotting typical of the genus, for a cleaner, more luminous late-season display. Burgundy-tinted arching stems add further color contrast against the oversized leaves. Grow it in consistently moist, humus-rich soil and avoid letting the ground dry out, since wilted foliage is slow to recover; established clumps can be divided in spring every few years to control spread and propagate.

common_name: Haldon Grange Lily of the Valley (Bold Gold-Edged Variegated Convallaria)

planting.note: Plant pips shallowly in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; the crown should rest just at or barely below soil level, and some morning light helps set the strongest gold edging.

directions: Plant pips shallowly in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Haldon Grange is named for the English garden where it was selected and bears broader, more brushstroke-like golden-cream leaf margins than most other variegated lily of the valley cultivars, on leaves that also run slightly larger than the straight species. The familiar arching sprays of small, intensely fragrant, pure white pendant bells open in late spring above the variegated foliage, followed later by small orange-red berries. Like other forms of lily of the valley it spreads readily by underground rhizomes into a dense, weed-suppressing colony and goes dormant by mid to late summer. Best sited in cool, humus-rich woodland soil where a touch of morning sun intensifies the gold leaf edging without scorching it; all parts of the plant are highly toxic if ingested.
